subject: English
topic: Fill in the blanks (grammar) — mixed tiers
description: Choose correct grammar form: tense, preposition, modal, conjunction

questions.stem: Fill in the blank: 'She has been working here ___ five years.'

options.option_text: Since, with a starting point
For, with a duration of time
From, with a starting point too
In, used at a fixed time only

questions.explanation: FOR = used with DURATION (period of time): for 5 years, for 2 hours, for a long time. SINCE = used with a STARTING POINT (specific moment in time): since 2020, since Monday, since I came. 'Five years' is a duration → use FOR. SSC PYQ favourite. Memory: 'For-Duration / Since-Starting-point'.

questions.stem: Fill in: 'If I ___ a millionaire, I would buy a yacht.'

options.option_text: Am, present-tense indicative form
Were, the subjunctive 'unreal' form
Will be, the future-tense form
Was, the past-tense form here

questions.explanation: SECOND CONDITIONAL (unreal/hypothetical present situation): If + past simple (or 'were' for all subjects), would + base. 'Were' is the SUBJUNCTIVE used for unreal conditions, even with I/he/she/it. 'If I were rich' (formal/correct) vs 'If I was rich' (colloquial). Other formulas: 1st CONDITIONAL (real future) = if + present, will + base ('If it rains, I will stay'). 3rd CONDITIONAL (unreal past) = if + had + V3, would have + V3.

questions.stem: Fill in: 'The book is ___ the table.'

options.option_text: In, used for inside an enclosed space
On, when contact with surface above
At, used for a precise location point
By, meaning beside or near to

questions.explanation: ON = surface contact (book ON table, picture ON wall, ring ON finger). IN = inside enclosed space (key IN drawer, water IN bottle). AT = at a specific point/place (at the bus stop, at home, at the door). BY = next to / near (sit by the window). All are PREPOSITIONS OF PLACE — most-tested in SSC + banking exams.

questions.stem: Fill in: 'Neither John ___ his brothers ___ available today.'

options.option_text: Or / are, the parallel form here used
Nor / are, agreeing with nearest subject
Nor / is, the singular verb form used
Or / is, the mixed standard form used

questions.explanation: NEITHER ... NOR (correlative pair). The verb agrees with the SUBJECT NEAREST to it (proximity rule). Here, 'his brothers' (plural) is nearest → 'are'. If reversed: 'Neither his brothers nor John IS available' (singular John nearest → 'is'). EITHER ... OR follows same rule. Distractor 1 — 'or' wrong (must be 'nor'). Distractor 3 — wrong agreement.

questions.stem: Fill in: 'I ___ rather stay at home tonight.'

options.option_text: Will, simple future tense form
Would, with 'rather' for preference
Should, expressing duty here
Could, expressing ability here

questions.explanation: 'WOULD RATHER' = expression of PREFERENCE. Followed by base verb (without 'to'). 'I would rather stay' = I prefer to stay. Same pattern: 'I had better leave' (had better + base). 'I'd rather not go' = preference not to. Cannot use 'will rather' or 'should rather' — these are wrong. Distractor 4 'could rather' also incorrect English.

questions.stem: Fill in: 'He works ___ a software engineer in Bangalore.'

options.option_text: Like a software engineer in Bangalore
As a software engineer in Bangalore
For a software engineer in Bangalore
On a software engineer in Bangalore

questions.explanation: AS = identity / role / profession ('he works AS an engineer' = he is one). LIKE = comparison ('he works LIKE a robot' = behaves similarly to one, but isn't one). LIKE/AS distinction is heavily tested. 'As' for jobs/roles ('appointed as captain'); 'like' for similes ('she runs LIKE a deer').

questions.stem: Fill in: 'Hardly had I entered the room ___ the lights went off.'

options.option_text: Then, used after a long pause
When, completing 'Hardly had ...'
Than, after comparative form
And, used for joining clauses

questions.explanation: Inverted pattern: HARDLY HAD ... WHEN ... = means one thing happened immediately followed by another. SCARCELY HAD ... WHEN ... (same construction). Compare: NO SOONER HAD ... THAN ... (uses 'than', not 'when'). 'No sooner had I entered THAN the lights went off.' Strict pairing: hardly/scarcely → when; no sooner → than. Common SSC trap: testing 'hardly...than' (wrong) or 'no sooner...when' (wrong).

questions.stem: Mount Everest, the highest peak in the world, lies in ___ Himalayas, which stretch across five nations.

options.option_text: a, which applies before singular countable nouns in context
an, used before nouns or noun phrases starting with a vowel sound
the, used with mountain ranges and unique geographical features
no article, as most geographical proper nouns require none

questions.explanation: The definite article 'the' is mandatory before names of mountain ranges (the Himalayas, the Alps, the Andes). Option D is the main distractor — while some geographical names take no article (India, Europe), plural mountain ranges always require 'the'. Options A and B are clearly inapplicable as Himalayas is neither a singular countable noun needing 'a' nor does it begin with a vowel sound.

questions.stem: She ___ to visit her grandparents every summer when she was a child, but she rarely does so now.

options.option_text: used, indicating a former regular habit or discontinued past practice
was used, forming a passive construction that distorts the meaning
is used, describing a present habitual tendency or current routine
would use, suggesting a conditional or imagined hypothetical action

questions.explanation: 'Used to + infinitive' expresses a past habit that no longer exists — exactly confirmed by 'but she rarely does so now.' Option B ('was used to') requires a gerund, not an infinitive: correct form would be 'was used to visiting.' Option C describes present familiarity, not a discontinued past habit. Option D ('would + base') can express past habits but only in narrative context, not with an infinitive phrase structured this way.

questions.stem: Either the principal or the teachers ___ responsible for maintaining discipline in this institution.

options.option_text: are, because the verb agrees with the nearest subject 'teachers'
is, because 'either...or' consistently takes only a singular verb
were, shifting the entire tense to past without any contextual basis
have been, inserting present perfect for a supposedly ongoing duty

questions.explanation: With 'either...or' and 'neither...nor', the verb agrees with the subject closest to it — the proximity rule. 'Teachers' is plural and nearest to the verb, so 'are' is correct. Option B is the most common error: students wrongly treat 'either...or' as always mandating a singular verb. The rule is proximity-based, not fixed-number-based.

questions.stem: The manager told the employees that the new branch ___ operational by the end of the following month.

options.option_text: will become, used in direct speech to express a definite future plan
becomes, used in zero conditional clauses for universal factual truths
had become, using past perfect for events completed before the speech time
would become, as indirect speech backshifts the present tense 'will' to 'would'

questions.explanation: In reported speech, the past reporting verb 'told' triggers tense backshift: 'will' becomes 'would.' Option A ('will become') is the original direct speech form and cannot stand inside a reported clause. Option C ('had become') would wrongly imply the branch was already operational before the manager even spoke — a timeline contradiction. Option B ('becomes') is used for timeless facts, not future plans.

questions.stem: He speaks ___ he knows everything about the subject, but he is actually a complete novice.

options.option_text: like, which informally precedes a noun or pronoun, not a full clause
as if, introducing a hypothetical or contrary-to-fact manner clause
as, correctly showing the real and actual manner of the action here
so that, which introduces a clause expressing purpose or end result

questions.explanation: 'As if' introduces an unreal or hypothetical comparison — here, the second clause ('but he is actually a novice') confirms the situation is contrary to fact. 'As' would mean he genuinely knows everything, contradicting the sentence. 'Like' governs noun/pronoun comparisons, not clauses with a subject and verb. 'So that' signals purpose, which is entirely unrelated here.

questions.stem: The committee recommended that every participant ___ a written report within three working days of the session.

options.option_text: submits, applying the indicative third-person singular present tense
submitted, backshifting the tense to agree with 'recommended' in past
submit, using the mandative subjunctive required after 'recommended'
would submit, inserting a conditional modal into a directive structure

questions.explanation: After verbs of recommendation, suggestion, or demand (recommend, suggest, insist, demand, require), the mandative subjunctive — 'that + subject + bare infinitive' — is mandatory regardless of the subject or the tense of the main clause. The base form 'submit' (without -s) is correct. Option A ('submits') is the most tempting distractor because 'every participant' is third-person singular, but the subjunctive overrides normal subject-verb concord. Option B wrongly applies reported-speech backshift logic, which does not govern subjunctive clauses.

questions.stem: Not until the audit report was made public ___ the full scale of the financial irregularities.

options.option_text: the board realised, retaining the normal declarative subject-verb order
did the board realise, with subject-auxiliary inversion after fronted negative
had the board realised, applying past-perfect inversion as in conditionals
the board had realised, keeping the past perfect without any inversion

questions.explanation: When a negative or restrictive adverbial ('not until', 'never', 'seldom', 'only when') is fronted to the sentence-initial position, subject-auxiliary inversion is grammatically compulsory. The correct pattern is: 'Not until X … did + subject + base verb.' Option C mimics the inversion found in unreal conditionals ('Had he known…'), which is a structurally different construction. Options A and D preserve normal declarative word order, which is ungrammatical after a fronted negative adverbial.
